title: Voices the Enemy Could Not Crack

passage.title: Voices the Enemy Could Not Crack
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Bank
passage.text:
During World War II, radio waves across the wide sea carried urgent orders between ships and island beaches. Yet each time a Marine spoke into a mic, sharp enemy ears tuned in on the same channel. Standard machine codes took half an hour to punch out on paper tape and read at the far end. Worse still, smart codebreakers often cracked those number patterns before the first small boats hit the sand. Fleet leaders needed a fast voice code that no foe could ever solve.

In 1942, twenty-nine young Navajo men met inside a locked room at a Marine camp on the west coast. Their spoken tongue had never been written down in books or taught to outside scholars. Its strict verb forms and rising or falling voice tones changed the sense of a word right away. Even a fluent speaker from a nearby tribe could not guess what a phrase meant without years of study. Starting from scratch, the young men built a two-part voice cipher locked inside their native speech.

The first layer used nature words to name modern war tools that did not exist in old camp life. Warplanes became birds: a fast dive plane was called a hawk, while a night scout plane was an owl. Big ships took the names of sea life, so a deep sub became an iron fish and a huge ship became a whale. Even if a spy knew a few words of the tongue, hearing that an iron fish struck a whale made no sense.

For names of islands or base camps that had no single code word, the men built a second layer. Inside the guarded wooden hall at camp, a phonetic list of common Navajo nouns was learned by each recruit before the fleet sailed west. To spell the letter A, a speaker might say the word for ant, apple, or axe. Because each English letter had three distinct choices, repeat letters never sounded the same twice in a row.

Under heavy fire on rough beaches like Iwo Jima, two Code Talkers could send and read a three-line order in twenty seconds. Machine ciphers needed thirty minutes to handle the exact same warning. Through the whole war, not one radio call sent in the Navajo code was ever broken by enemy teams. By blending old grammar with clever wordplay, those Marine radio crews forged the safest voice shield in history.

tier2Words.definition: Able to speak or understand a language smoothly, easily, and accurately
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin 'fluere' meaning to flow smoothly
tier2Words.contextClue: Even someone who spoke a nearby tribal language smoothly could not guess Navajo voice tones.

tier2Words.definition: A secret system of writing or speaking used to hide the true meaning of messages
tier2Words.rootHint: From Arabic 'sifr', later used for secret number and letter codes
tier2Words.contextClue: The recruits built a two-part secret code system locked inside their native speech.

tier2Words.definition: Based on spoken sounds and how letters are pronounced
tier2Words.rootHint: From Greek 'phone' meaning voice or sound
tier2Words.contextClue: To spell out letters by sound, speakers used Navajo nouns whose English meanings started with each letter.

tier2Words.definition: Built or shaped something strong and lasting through hard effort
tier2Words.rootHint: From a blacksmith's forge where hot metal is hammered into strong tools
tier2Words.contextClue: By blending old grammar with clever wordplay, the Marines created the safest voice shield.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"Inside the guarded wooden hall at camp, a phonetic list of common Navajo nouns was learned by each recruit before the fleet sailed west."

Who performed the action of learning the phonetic list in this sentence?

options.text: The common Navajo nouns inside the guarded wooden hall
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice flips the action! The list of Navajo nouns is what was learned, not who did the learning.

options.text: Each recruit training at the Marine camp
options.childFeedback: Spot on! In Paragraph 4, the words 'by each recruit' right after 'was learned' show that each Marine recruit learned the phonetic list.

options.text: The fleet that sailed west across the sea
options.childFeedback: Watch out—'before the fleet sailed west' only tells when the training happened in Paragraph 4, not who learned the list.

options.text: Enemy listeners tuning in on the radio channel
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraphs 2 and 5 explain that enemy listeners could never understand or learn the Navajo code.

questions.provingSentenceText: Inside the guarded wooden hall at camp, a phonetic list of common Navajo nouns was learned by each recruit before the fleet sailed west.
questions.childTip: Spot on! In Paragraph 4, the words 'by each recruit' right after 'was learned' show that each Marine recruit learned the phonetic list.
questions.parentExplanation: The subject 'a phonetic list of common Navajo nouns' receives the passive verb 'was learned.' The agent performing the action is 'each recruit.'
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 4, spot the action phrase 'was learned' and look right after 'by' to find who did the learning.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 5:

"By blending old grammar with clever wordplay, those Marine radio crews forged the safest voice shield in history."

What does the word "forged" most nearly mean as used in this sentence?

options.text: Created and built through careful effort
options.childFeedback: Spot on! In Paragraph 5, 'forged the safest voice shield' compares the Marines' careful code-building to a blacksmith shaping strong metal.

options.text: Copied illegally from an enemy codebook
options.childFeedback: Careful—while 'forge' can mean fake in other situations, Paragraph 2 shows the Navajo Marines created their own original code.

options.text: Melted down inside a hot ship engine
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice takes metalworking too literally; no radio equipment was melted inside a ship engine.

options.text: Forgot completely after the war ended
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice contradicts Paragraph 5, which celebrates how the code saved thousands of lives and remained unbroken.

questions.provingSentenceText: By blending old grammar with clever wordplay, those Marine radio crews forged the safest voice shield in history.
questions.childTip: Spot on! In Paragraph 5, 'forged the safest voice shield' compares the Marines' careful code-building to a blacksmith shaping strong metal.
questions.parentExplanation: While 'forge' can mean faking a signature in other contexts, here 'forged the safest voice shield' draws on a blacksmith shaping strong metal, meaning built or crafted.
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 5, think of how a blacksmith shapes strong metal—here, the Marines built a strong code by blending grammar and wordplay.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 4, why did the Code Talkers assign three distinct Navajo words to each English letter?

options.text: Because the Navajo language only had three nouns for animals and plants
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice makes an extreme, false claim; the Navajo language is rich and complex, and recruits chose from many nature words.

options.text: Because three different Marines had to speak into the radio mic at the exact same time
options.childFeedback: Careful—Paragraph 5 explains that two Code Talkers sent and read orders between locations, not three Marines talking into one mic at once.

options.text: So that repeated letters in a spelled word would not make the same sound pattern twice in a row
options.childFeedback: Spot on! Paragraph 4 explains that having three different Navajo word choices for each letter stopped repeated letters from creating a pattern enemy codebreakers could spot.

options.text: So that machine tape printers could punch three holes for every vowel
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraphs 1 and 2 explain that the Navajo voice cipher replaced slow machine tape printers altogether.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because each English letter had three distinct choices, repeat letters never sounded the same twice in a row.
questions.childTip: Spot on! Paragraph 4 explains that having three different Navajo word choices for each letter stopped repeated letters from creating a pattern enemy codebreakers could spot.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 4, the author explains that giving each letter three distinct choices prevented recurring letter patterns that enemy codebreakers normally look for.
questions.retryHint: Look in Paragraph 4 for the sentence that explains the benefit of having three distinct choices per letter.

questions.prompt: How are Paragraphs 3 and 4 organized to explain how the Navajo code worked?

options.text: They compare the speed of deep subs with the flight speed of night scout planes.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—Paragraph 3 mentions subs ('iron fish') and planes ('birds') as code examples, not to compare their travel speeds.

options.text: They explain the two cipher layers: nature words for war tools and a phonetic list for spelling.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! Paragraph 3 explains the first layer of nature words for war terms, and Paragraph 4 explains the second layer of phonetic words for spelling names.

options.text: They list every island battle in the exact order the fleet visited them.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—Paragraphs 3 and 4 explain how the two code layers worked rather than listing a timeline of island battles.

options.text: They argue that machine ciphers were much safer than spoken codes during island landings.
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice reverses the article's main point; spoken Navajo code was much faster and safer than machine ciphers.

questions.provingSentenceText: The first layer used nature words to name modern war tools that did not exist in old camp life.
questions.childTip: Spot on! Paragraph 3 explains the first layer of nature words for war terms, and Paragraph 4 explains the second layer of phonetic words for spelling names.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 introduces a 'two-part voice cipher,' and Paragraphs 3 and 4 systematically unpack each layer: nature words for whole war terms (Paragraph 3) and a multi-option phonetic list for spelling names (Paragraph 4).
questions.retryHint: Notice how Paragraph 3 starts with 'The first layer' and Paragraph 4 explains 'a second layer.'

questions.prompt: Part A: Why was the Navajo code a major improvement over standard military machine codes during battle?

options.text: It allowed Marines to send unbreakable orders in seconds instead of waiting half an hour for machine tape.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! Paragraphs 1 and 5 show that machine codes took thirty minutes to punch and decode, while Navajo Code Talkers sent unbreakable orders in just twenty seconds.

options.text: It worked without any radio sets by flashing mirrors between ships and beaches.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraphs 2 and 5 clearly state that the Code Talkers spoke over field radio sets, not with flashing mirrors.

options.text: It was printed in books so every sailor in the fleet could read it without training.
options.childFeedback: Careful—Paragraph 4 states that no codebooks were ever printed on paper, because each recruit memorized the entire list.

options.text: It automatically jammed enemy radio channels so nobody else on the sea could speak.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 2 notes that enemy listeners could still hear the voices on the channel, even though they could not crack their meaning.

questions.provingSentenceText: Under heavy fire on rough beaches like Iwo Jima, two Code Talkers could send and read a three-line order in twenty seconds.
questions.childTip: Spot on! Paragraphs 1 and 5 show that machine codes took thirty minutes to punch and decode, while Navajo Code Talkers sent unbreakable orders in just twenty seconds.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraphs 1 and 5 contrast slow, vulnerable machine codes (30 minutes) with the Navajo code, which sent unbreakable three-line orders in just 20 seconds.
questions.retryHint: Compare the time it took two Code Talkers in Paragraph 5 against the thirty minutes needed for machine codes.

questions.prompt: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "In 1942, twenty-nine young Navajo men met inside a locked room at a Marine camp on the west coast."
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this detail from Paragraph 2 only tells when and where the first twenty-nine recruits met.

options.text: "Warplanes became birds: a fast dive plane was called a hawk, while a night scout plane was an owl."
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this example from Paragraph 3 only shows which bird names stood for warplanes, not how the code improved battle speed.

options.text: "To spell the letter A, a speaker might say the word for ant, apple, or axe."
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this line from Paragraph 4 only gives three code words for the letter A rather than comparing the code to machine ciphers.

options.text: "Under heavy fire on rough beaches like Iwo Jima, two Code Talkers could send and read a three-line order in twenty seconds."
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This quote from Paragraph 5 directly proves Question 5 by showing that Code Talkers could send and read a three-line order in just twenty seconds.

questions.provingSentenceText: Under heavy fire on rough beaches like Iwo Jima, two Code Talkers could send and read a three-line order in twenty seconds.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This quote from Paragraph 5 directly proves Question 5 by showing that Code Talkers could send and read a three-line order in just twenty seconds.
